teaching.h: Why gender is the first thing to learn in Russian
teaching.p: Every Russian noun is masculine, feminine, or neuter, and this choice ripples into adjective endings, past-tense verbs, and more — getting gender right early saves a lot of confusion later. The good news: the ending usually tells you which one.

teaching.h: Masculine — usually a bare consonant ending
Feminine — usually -а or -я
Neuter — usually -о or -е

teaching.h: Why Russian has cases at all
teaching.p: Like German, Russian shows a noun's grammatical role by changing its ENDING rather than relying only on word order — which is exactly why Russian sentences can rearrange more freely than English ones and still make sense.

teaching.h: Nominative — the subject, dictionary form
teaching.p: This is the 'default' form you'd look up in a dictionary.

teaching.h: Accusative — the direct object
The other four, briefly
teaching.p: Genitive shows possession ('of'), dative shows the indirect object ('to/for'), instrumental shows means ('by/with'), and prepositional is used for location or topic ('about/in'). Each of the next several lessons builds on this foundation.

teaching.h: Two conjugation patterns, and you learn which one per verb
teaching.p: Every Russian verb belongs to Conjugation I or Conjugation II — the ending pattern tells you which, and once you know the type, the whole conjugation is predictable.

teaching.h: Conjugation I example
teaching.ex: читать → читаю, читаешь, читает, читаем, читаете, читают
teaching.exTranslation: to read → I read, you read, he/she reads, we read, you all read, they read

teaching.h: Conjugation II example
teaching.ex: говорить → говорю, говоришь, говорит, говорим, говорите, говорят
teaching.exTranslation: to speak → I speak, you speak, he/she speaks, we speak, you all speak, they speak

teaching.h: Present-tense sentences often skip 'to be' entirely
teaching.p: Unlike English, which always needs 'am/is/are', Russian usually just drops the verb 'to be' in present-tense statements — the sentence still makes complete sense without it.
teaching.exTranslation: I am a student. (literally: I student)

teaching.h: Why adjective endings change so much
teaching.p: Since the noun itself already tells you gender, the adjective describing it has to match — this is the same underlying logic as German and Spanish adjective agreement, just with Russian's own set of endings.

teaching.h: Masculine ending: -ый/-ой
Feminine ending: -ая
Neuter ending: -ое

quiz.q: Adjectives in Russian must agree in:
Which ending typically marks a feminine adjective?

teaching.h: A distinction English speakers have to build a new instinct for
teaching.p: Russian doesn't just mark WHEN an action happened — nearly every verb comes in an imperfective/perfective PAIR, marking whether the action is ongoing/repeated or a single completed event. Choosing the right one is genuinely one of the harder parts of Russian for English speakers.

teaching.h: Imperfective — process, repetition, ongoing
Perfective — one completed action, often with a clear result
Perfective verbs don't have a present tense
teaching.p: This is a genuinely useful fact for narrowing down which form you need: perfective verbs only exist in past and future forms, since 'a completed action happening right now' is a contradiction.

teaching.h: Why parts of speech connect directly to case and agreement
teaching.p: In Russian, knowing a word's category tells you exactly what it's required to do grammatically — nouns decline by case, adjectives must agree with their noun, but adverbs stay frozen.

teaching.h: Nouns themselves change form based on case
teaching.p: This is the practical payoff of everything from Lesson 2 — the noun isn't just labeled with a case, its actual ENDING changes.
teaching.exTranslation: table (nominative) → of the table (genitive) → to the table (dative)

teaching.h: Adverbs, refreshingly, never change
teaching.p: Unlike adjectives, which must match gender/case/number, adverbs are invariable — one form, used everywhere.
teaching.exTranslation: quickly — always the same, no matter the sentence

teaching.h: Each preposition demands a specific case
teaching.p: You can't just pick any case after a preposition — each one requires a particular case for the noun that follows, and this pairing has to be memorized alongside the preposition itself.

quiz.q: In "Он бежит быстро," what part of speech is "быстро"?
Do Russian nouns change form based on case?

teaching.h: Повествовательное — the plain statement
Вопросительное — the question
teaching.p: In spoken Russian, a question is often formed with the exact same word order as a statement, just with rising intonation — no verb-flip required like in German.

teaching.h: Побудительное — the command
teaching.p: Uses the imperative verb form, directly instructing someone.

teaching.h: Сложное предложение — combining ideas
teaching.p: и (and), но (but), потому что (because) connect clauses, similar to English/German connectors.
teaching.ex: Я люблю кошек, но у меня есть собака.
teaching.exTranslation: I love cats, but I have a dog.

quiz.q: "Сядь, пожалуйста." is an example of a:
Я люблю кошек, ___ у меня есть собака. (but)
In spoken Russian, questions are often signaled by:

teaching.h: Why Russian needs FOUR words for 'to go'
teaching.p: This genuinely trips up learners: Russian distinguishes not just walking vs. by-vehicle, but also a single specific trip vs. habitual/repeated travel. Four separate verbs cover what English handles with just 'go'.

teaching.h: идти vs. ходить — walking, right now vs. habitually
teaching.ex: Я иду в школу. Я хожу в школу каждый день.
teaching.exTranslation: I am going to school (right now). I go to school every day (habitually).

teaching.h: ехать vs. ездить — the same split, but by vehicle
teaching.ex: Я еду на работу. Я езжу на работу каждый день.
teaching.exTranslation: I am going to work (right now, by vehicle). I go to work every day (by vehicle, habitually).

teaching.h: Prefixes change the meaning further
teaching.p: при- (arriving), у- (leaving), пере- (crossing) attach to these motion-verb roots to specify direction even more precisely.
teaching.exTranslation: to arrive (on foot), to leave (on foot)

quiz.q: Which verb describes going somewhere right now, on foot?
Я ___ в школу каждый день. (habitual, on foot)
Я ___ на работу каждый день. (habitual, by vehicle)

teaching.h: Simple comparative — a predictable ending change
чем introduces the comparison, like English 'than'
самый + adjective forms the superlative
teaching.p: самый agrees in gender/case with the noun it describes.

teaching.h: A few common irregulars
teaching.p: Just like English's good/better/best breaks the normal pattern, a handful of high-frequency Russian adjectives do too.

teaching.h: Real conditions — plain present/future with если
teaching.p: For realistic situations, если (if) pairs with normal present or future tense, no special mood needed.
teaching.ex: Если пойдёт дождь, я останусь дома.
teaching.exTranslation: If it rains, I'll stay home.

teaching.h: Hypothetical conditions — a single flexible particle
teaching.p: Unlike English, Spanish, or German (which have distinct structures for present vs. past hypotheticals), Russian just uses если бы plus a past-tense-form verb, for BOTH cases — genuinely simpler once you know this.
teaching.ex: Если бы у меня было время, я бы поехал.
teaching.exTranslation: If I had time, I would go.

teaching.h: бы doesn't care what time you're imagining
teaching.p: The particle бы attaches to a past-form verb purely to signal 'this is hypothetical' — it's not actually marking past time at all, which is why it works equally for present and past hypotheticals.

teaching.h: бы can move around in the sentence
teaching.p: Its position is flexible, but the если...бы structure remains recognizable wherever it lands.
teaching.ex: Я бы поехал, если бы у меня было время.
teaching.exTranslation: I would go, if I had time.

quiz.q: Если ___ у меня было время, я бы поехал. (бы)
Does Russian conditional distinguish present vs. past hypothetical like English does?
options: No, бы works the same either way
quiz.answer: No, бы works the same either way

quiz.q: бы attaches to a verb in which form?

teaching.h: Словосочетание — a chunk with no independent subject-verb pairing
Придаточное предложение — depends on the main clause
который — introducing a relative clause
teaching.p: Agrees with the noun it describes in gender and number, similar to German's der/die/das relative pronouns.
teaching.exTranslation: The person who called is my teacher.

teaching.h: Commas before subordinate clauses are mandatory
teaching.p: Unlike English, where this comma is sometimes optional stylistically, Russian requires it every time — not a stylistic choice.
teaching.exTranslation: I know that you are tired.

quiz.q: "новый дом" is an example of a:
который agrees with the noun it describes in:
Are subordinate clauses always set off by a comma in Russian?

teaching.h: Действительный залог — the default
The informal -ся passive
teaching.p: A verb ending in -ся often carries passive-like meaning in casual usage — this is the version you'll hear far more often.
teaching.exTranslation: The food is being cooked by the chef.

teaching.h: The formal passive, with participles
teaching.p: Past passive participle + a form of быть — this version shows up mainly in formal or written Russian.
teaching.exTranslation: The food was cooked by the chef.

teaching.h: Register matters here
teaching.p: Casual spoken Russian actually prefers active voice most of the time — passive constructions lean formal/written.

quiz.q: Which register more often uses passive voice?

teaching.h: Прямая речь — the exact words
Косвенная речь — reporting with что
teaching.p: Similar structure to English's 'that' clause.
teaching.exTranslation: She said that she was tired.

teaching.h: No tense backshift needed — different from English
teaching.p: This is genuinely easier than English: Russian typically KEEPS the original tense when reporting speech, rather than shifting it further into the past.
teaching.ex: "Я иду домой" → Он сказал, что идёт домой.
teaching.exTranslation: "I'm going home" → He said that he's going home. (present tense kept)

teaching.h: Pronouns still shift, same as other languages
teaching.ex: "Я устал" → Он сказал, что он устал.
teaching.exTranslation: "I'm tired" → He said that he was tired.

quiz.q: Does Russian shift tense backward in reported speech, like English?
options: No, tense usually stays the same
quiz.answer: No, tense usually stays the same

teaching.h: Comma requirements are stricter than in English
teaching.p: Before что, потому что, который, если, and similar subordinators, a comma is mandatory — no stylistic flexibility here, unlike English.

teaching.h: A dash instead of quotation marks for dialogue
teaching.p: Where English encloses speech in quotation marks, Russian often just uses a dash at the start of the line — a genuinely different visual convention.

teaching.h: Less capitalization than English overall
teaching.p: Days, months, nationalities all stay lowercase — matching the same pattern you saw in Spanish.

teaching.h: ё vs. е — a small mark with real consequences
teaching.p: ё is often written as plain е in casual text, but the two represent different sounds and can distinguish entirely different words.

teaching.h: Two verb forms English handles very differently
teaching.p: Both let you pack more information into a sentence without adding a whole new clause — a genuinely efficient feature of literary Russian.

teaching.h: Причастие — a verb acting as an adjective
teaching.p: Agrees with its noun in gender, case, and number, just like a regular adjective.
teaching.exTranslation: the reading person / a person who is reading

teaching.h: Past passive participles are especially common
teaching.p: Describe something that had an action done to it.

teaching.h: Деепричастие — a verb acting as an adverb, and never changing form
teaching.p: Unlike причастие, this form is invariable — it doesn't agree with anything, since it's describing the ACTION, not a noun.
teaching.exTranslation: while reading the book, he smiled

quiz.q: ___ книга (the book that was read — participle)
Does деепричастие agree with gender/case like причастие does?

teaching.h: Why these words matter for sounding fluent
teaching.p: Same role as in every other language in this course — they show HOW ideas connect, rather than just listing facts one after another.

teaching.h: однако — contrast
teaching.ex: Он старался. Однако, у него не получилось.
teaching.exTranslation: He tried. However, it didn't work out.

teaching.h: поэтому — cause and result
teaching.ex: Шёл сильный дождь, поэтому матч отменили.
teaching.exTranslation: It was raining heavily, therefore the match was cancelled.

teaching.h: кроме того — adding a point
teaching.ex: Она умная. Кроме того, она очень трудолюбивая.
teaching.exTranslation: She's smart. Furthermore, she's very hardworking.
